speechtext: Assuming that the stock which we may call the exchangeable stock to distinguish it from the other stock, which we may call the retained stock, because it is retained in the possession of the stockholders, is worth $50,000,000, the Government takes that $50,000,000 of stock and regards that as its possession. Is that right?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
No. The Government
takes the $180,000,000 of stock. It gets in every dollar of stock that is outstanding and gives in exchange, if you wish to put it that way, $50,000,000, if that is the award of the arbitrators, of this new stock bearing interest at four per cent, and guaranteed by the Government, but without any voting power.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: What the Government takes is what the arbitrators express to be the value of the exchangeable stock.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: They take the whole of it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: But what they get in value is the value the arbitrators put upon the stock. Is it not the case that the Government gives in exchange an equal amount of guaranteed four per cent stock to the holders of this exchangeable stock?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: No, we give stock to the amount of the award.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: That is what I say: $50,000,000, if that was the amount of, the award.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: For the sake of illustration, let us suppose the amount is $60,000,000, which is just one third of $180,000,000.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Make it ten millions.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Well, let us split the difference and say twenty, with the advantage on our side.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Always.
. Mr. ROWELL: Say twenty millions, that is, one-ninth of the stock outstanding. Let us assume that it is all of equal value, although as a matter of fact it is not. It would mean that a man for nine shares of stock surrendered of the par value of nine hundred dollars would receive one share of one hundred dollars of non-votable stock, on which the Government guarantees to pay four per cent interest half-yearly. That is the situation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The Government gets nothing that he does not get the equivalent of.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The Government only
gives him in return what the arbitrators find to be the value of the stock, and the one share should represent the value of the nine.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Exactly.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The value of the one should be equal to the value of the nine, with this difference, which is an important one:	At the present time, if we paid in
actual value, having regard to what money is worth, we would have to pay more than on the basis of four per cent. On the present value of money we would have to give him a security bearing, say, five and a half per cent. But we do not discharge it in that way. ^ We discharge it by a four per cent security, so that he does not really get the value. It is a very great saving to the country. It is one of the important features oi the agreement that we are able to discharge our obligation by a four per cent security instead of five and a half per cent at the present rate.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If that point is disposed of I should like to bring another to the attention of the committee. Some one owns this railroad. Apparently it is not the Government but the Grand Trunk Railway Company, which is to continue to own it. Am I right?

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Don't answer too hastily. The Government do not own it.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The shareholders own it, and the shareholders will be the Government of Canada. They will own it the same as they do the Canadian Northern.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Will not the Grand Tiunk Railway Company of Canada remain an entity?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Certainly, but it cannot exist without shareholders, and all the stock being transferred to the Canadian Government, the Government are therefore the owners of the railway.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I am not discussing that point; I am endeavouring to ascertain how this matter will work out. There are one or two things which we know very well. For instance, we know that we shall have the elephant, and secondly we know that we shall have to feed him; but I am not sure that we all know how he is to be handled. If the Grand Trunk Railway Company remains a corporate entity, of course it will have shareholders. There is going to be $180,000,000 of these several classes of preferred and common stock which are to be arbitrated on and called in. Are they to be cancelled, or do they still remain stock of the Grand Trunk Railway Company? There is going to be $60,000,000 of guaranteed stock which will remain outstanding. There is no question about that; and there will be ten, twenty, thirty or fifty millions of new guaranteed stock issued. Do all the stocks called in remain in the Treasury of Canada? Are we to have the Grand Trunk Railway Company? Is my hon. friend the Minister of Railways to be president of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and are we to have an annual meeting for the proper conduct of the business? The Government do not own the road, but some one must own it. The Government do not own it except as stockholders, and they can only be stockholders in a corporate body. I am not complaining; I am only trying, in the calm serenity of this sunny afternoon, to learn something. It seems to me that we are perpetuating the Grand 'Trunk Railway Company. Is my hon. friend (Mr. J. D. Reid) to be president, and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Rowell) to be vice-president of the company, with all the paraphernalia of the Grand Trunk Railway Company kept in existence?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
That is exactly the point I made in answer to my hon. friend the

leader of the Opposition. There are two methods of ownership, one by holding stock in the company, and the other by owning the property. In this case we own it by stock in the company. The $180,000,000 is not to be cancelled. Whatever may be decided in the future, at the present time it is the intention to preserve the corporate entity of the Grand Trunk, which carries all the franchises and privileges and agreements with it. But the management, as .my hon. friend has pointed out, will be in the reorganized Board of the Canadian National railways which will operate all the Government railways as one system. Probably in time it may be wise to bring about actual consolidation: it may be wise to bring about a practical merging. That is a question of policy that will have to be settled according to the developments of the situation from time to time.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I am not trying to argue against my hon. friend, or to determine what is Vight. We are all anxious to ascertain where we are at, to use the popular slang expression. It is perfectly clear that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is to be perpetuated; it is to own this property. We are the shareholders in the Grand Trunk Company; I admit the force of that statement. But it is well that the public should understand that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is not to be wiped out. It is to exist; all its franchise, powers and authorities are to remain, and they are to be exercised by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and others. If the Government do not own the road it is clear enough that the Grand Trunk Railway Company, no matter who owns the shares, are still to be the owners, and we are to be shareholders in it. Let us clearly understand that this is a Bill to perpetuate the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and that we are to be its shareholders.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that the Canada Atlantic Railway was takqn over years ago.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Before the minister proceeds further, am I right or wrong?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The hon. member is right in that the Grand Trunk Railway Company is to be continued in existence.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: If the Grand Trunk is to he continued as a corporation, where is it to get its revenue?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I will answer the hon. member in a moment. I was going to say that the Canada Atlantic Company was

taken over 'by the Grand Trunk Railway and although you do not hear of the Canada Atlantic Company now it is still in existence as part of the Grand Trunk system. We are taking over the Grand Trunk Railway system and as shareholders we will own it. It is necessary to keep it in existence, but we transfer the operation of it, the same as the Canadian Northern and the Intercolonial, to the Canadian National Railway system, and they will all be operated as one system. All the revenues from the whole railway system will go into one fund to pay for their operation.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: All of them?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Under the Bill we passed last year. The stock, having been transferred to the Canadian National Railway system, it ia. owned by the Government, and the whole system will be owned and operated by the Government.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I am not quite clear in regard to the answer given to the hon. member for North Waterloo as to new issue of stock. The President of the Privy Council is corporation lawyer enough to know that you cannot issue new stock without getting value for it, at least according to Canadian law. You are increasing the stock to some extent by an issue of new stock.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I am lawyer enough to know that this Parliament, which creates a corporation, can authorize it to issue stock in any form that Parliament sees fit. This Bill expressly provides that we may issue this stock and it defines the position of the stock.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: In exchange for the other, but what about the increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue; Minister of Railways and Canals
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The common and the first, second and third preference stock is all transferred to the Government, and it is held by the Government. subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The minister himself introduced the subject of taxation and we must deal with it. Gentlemen who are so fond of public.ownership cannot have their cake and eat it. They must take the responsibilities of their love for public ownership. Public ownership means property in the Crown. That property shall become the property of the Crown representing the public. It is public owned property, meaning that it belongs to the Crown. There is no such thing as the Crown owning, and not owning property. It either owns the property or it does not. There is no use of camouflaging about it? It would not'be a fair defence for the Government to say: "We own the property but we have put it in our wives' names" so that our creditors cannot touch it. Is that a fair position for the Government to be in? The Government say that they own the property but to get out of some responsibility or liability they say that they are holding the property in somebody else's name. The courts of the country do not recognize camouflage of that kind. They go direct to the point and say "Who owns this property?" And whoever owns it has the rights and responsibilities incidental to it. If the contention of the Government is right this property belongs to the Crown when we take it over. I do not agree with what they say about stock or shares or bonds or anything else. If they take the bonds they are taking the property with it, and they own the whole thing, if we are to believe them, so that it is the property of the Crown. There is no [DOT] escaping from that conclusion. Now, section 125 of the British North America Act says:
No lands or property belonging to Canada or any province shall be liable to taxation.
We cannot change that, and we cannot put anything in this Bill-we can, but it would be mere child's play, because the courts would not recognize it-we cannot
fMr. Euler.] '
put anything in this Bill which will cor>-flict with the constitution. Now, this property that we are taking over-and the farmers might as well know it-must necessarily be public property, the property of the Crown, and therefore exempt from taxation under the British North America Act. How can it be otherwise? If it is not exempt from taxation it is not the property of the Crown, it is not public ownership. The Government must take one position or-the other. The President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) shakes his head, but I do not know of any Mahommet's coffin position he can take between Heaven and earth about this property: It is either owned privately or it is owned publicly. If it is owned publicly it cannot be taxed; if it is owned privately it can be taxed. The Government state that the municipalities in Ontario along the line of the Grand Trunk can collect taxes on the railway property. Does the President of the Council think that the good people of Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia are going to tolerate that discrimination against themselves? He will at once have to start paying taxes on the Intercolonial railway, because here is a government road running through the western provinces and the middle of Canada paying local taxes at every stage, but although we in the eastern provinces are supplying our share of the funds to run those railways, where the Intercolonial railway is operated not a cent of local taxes are paid in respect of its property. Is that a system of municipal management that the hon. gentleman thinks will stand for one moment? He is introducing a doctrine that, when applied throughout the country, is going to give him a lot of difficulty. I want to know at this stage: Is he ready to admit that the Government must pay municipal taxes in relation to the Intercolonial and its branches or in relation to any other road that is being operated in conjunction with the Intercolonial railway? If he says, No, then the people of the Maritime Provinces will say: We are furnishing our share of the money to run the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific, the Transcontinental and the Canadian Northern, and if those roads are paying taxes in the West they must pay us taxes in the East. I want to know from the Government if it is their intention to adopt this as a universal rule, that Government owned roads will pay taxes.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

I am not quite sure that I clearly understand my hon. friend's viewpoint in reference to this tax question. If

I rightly understand him, however, his argument is that the Intercolonial should be placed in all respects on the same basis as the Canadian Northern is at present and as the Grand Trunk will be under this arrangement. If my hon. friend takes that position, and if the freight and passenger rates on the Intercolonial are raised so as to bring them up- to the full standard charged on the other roads, I think possibly the Intercolonial could afford to pay taxes.

speechtext: Not at all.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: My friend must be content to say that the Intercolonial was built to serve a particular national purpose, and by reason of that fact the Maritime Provinces are entitled to rates below the normal standard charged on other roads, and therefore the railway property is not taxed; or he must be prepared to take the position that it shall in all respects stand on exactly the same basis as all the other road's. In the latter case I think the Intercolonial could probably afford to pay taxes to the municipalities. However, that question is not now before us.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: Certainly not.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
My hon. friend wants the assets without the liabilities-he wants to eat his cake and have it, too. Coming back to the other point, my hon. friend says that either the Government owns'the road or it does not; the property is subject to taxation or it is not. Does not he realize that the stock of the company is property in the hands of the shareholders; the physical assets of the company are property in the hands of the company? Both are subject to taxation, or the income from them would be so subject. If the holder of stock in the Grand Trunk lived in the province of Ontario and received dividends from his stock, he would be liable to taxation on those dividends while the Grand Trunk would be liable to taxation on its physical assets. Now, what we are buying under this Bill is the stock. That stock is vested
in the Government, and would not be liable to taxation, for being government property it is covered by the British North America Act. But when we come to the question of the physical assets, which are still vested in the corporate entity, that corporate entity being distinct from the shareholders they would still continue liable to taxation by the municipalities. The situation here does not differ in any respect from the Canadian Northern situation. The Government took over the stock of the 'Canadian Northern, and that stock is government property; it is not liable to taxation under the British North America Act. But the physical assets of the railway, which are still vested in the railway corporation, are at the present time taxed in the different municipalities throughout the Dominion. The Grand Trunk will be put in exactly the same position. The argument advanced by my hon. friend is that if the Government owns all the stock, therefore the intervention of the corporation between the stockholders and the Government does not change the real ownership, and the municipality therefore could not collect taxes. That is my hon. friend's suggestion. Well, we have had this practical experience with the Canadian Northern, that the municipalities have taxed the railway, and the taxes have been paid, on the ground I have mentioned, and the same ground will apply to the Grand Trunk.
Coming to the point of my hon. friend from North Waterloo-

However, the physical assets of this railway could not be transferred to the Govern-

rnent without the necessary legislation. If any government, therefore, decided, to wipe out the corporate entity of the -Grand Trunk and vest all its property in the Government, it would have to come down for legislation to do so, and on that occasion a provision might properly he inserted in the Bill to the effect that notwithstanding the change, local municipalities would stijl be entitled to levy taxes as if the property were owned by a corporate entity, the Grand Trunk But that is not necessary at this time.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
The clause in the Canadian Pacific Railway Company charter of 1880-81 to which I have reference is as follows:
The Canadian Pacific railway, and all stations and station grounds, work 6hops, buildings, yards and other property, rolling stock and appurtenances required and used for the construction and working thereof, and the capital stock of the company, shall be forever free from taxation by the Dominion, or by any province hereafter to be established, or by any municipal corporation therein; and the lands of the company, in the North West Territories, until they are either sold or occupied, shall also be free from such taxation for 20 years after the grant thereof from the Crown.	.
Hon. members will see that I was partly right and partly wrong. But in- view of the fact tha-t I am partly right, I contend that if the Canadian Pacific is to go scot-free until the crack of doom so far as taxes are concerned, the minister should not take the view that this new system should pay taxes. It is not right that the Canadian Pacific should -be free from taxes in the West

and the West is a very important part of Canada-while the Government railway system is taxed; the two should be in a position of absolute equality.

speechtext: It is my view that municipalities should have the right to tax railways, as well as farmers or -anybody else.

speechtext: They would not be yielding up any rights, -because under the constitution of the railway company these properties would be non^taxable. .

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
When were these lands
granted to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company? I observe that the exemption is for twenty years after the land was granted -by the Crown, and the land was surely granted more than twenty years ago.
Mr. RI-OHARDiSON: A lot of things have happened in this country that my hon. friend does not know anything about, in spite of his wide knowledge. The clause reads:
The lands of the company .... shall also be free from taxation for twenty years after the grant thereof from the Crown.
But the wily Canadian Pacific Railway Company allowed the twenty years to expire without taking out their patents, and then they claimed th-at " the grant thereof " meant the issue of patents. Of course, all the land-s that had been sold in the meantime became taxable and the burden of the tax fell upon the settler and the purchaser. Well, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company got a judicial decision, which I and other members resisted very strongly, giving them exemption for another twenty years, and by that time all the lands- will he sold.	.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
This question of taxation is a very important one. As the Minister of Railways has said-, there has been a good deal of apprehension among the municipalities that the physical assets of the Grand Trunk Railway Company will be exempted from municipal taxation. It has been established- by the President of the Council that as long as the -modus vivendi provided in the Bill continues, local taxation will continue. But there seems- to -be an element of doubt whether this will go on forever; it is suggested that at some future time the Government may decide- to vest 'the titles to the real estate in- the Crown, and these lands would, under the British North America Act, then be exempt from taxation.' We should have a definite statement from the Government that if they do vest in the Crown the real estate, lands, buildings and so on, now vested in the Grand Trunk Railway Company, they will see that no injustice is d-one to the -municipalities. There will be a good deal of dissatisfaction on the part of the municipalities if they get the idea that with the Grand Trunk property vested in the Crown it will be free from taxation for all time to corner I believe that under this Bill the property will be vested in the Crown; I can see absolute reason for saying t'h-at it is public property; it remains

public property under a corporation. One of the main reasons why it should be run under a corporation is because it operates in the United States as well as in Canada, and as a railway entity in the United States it might be able to do in the United States what the Canadian Government would find it very difficult to do. But I hope that the President of the Council will give the assurance, if it cannot be incorporated in the Bill, that if the question of municipal taxation does arise in connection with any future transfer to the Crown of the right of way, real estate and buildings pertaining to this system, the rights of the municipalities will be respected.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: My hon. friend evidently overlooked an observation I made. There can be no transfer to the Crown of the property and assets of this railway without new legislation. This legislation does not authorize it, and so long as the company continues its corporate entity it cannot dispose of its property and assets except under the terms of the Railway Act. If in the future the property was being transferred to the Crown that would be a proper *occasion upon which to provide, in the legislation then enacted, that the road *should^ be free from taxation. All we are doing in this case is exactly' what is now being done with respect to the Canadian Northern. The Government owns the stock; the Canadian Northern railway continues to pay taxes in the local municipalities through which the railway runs.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

It seems to me only fair if municipalities, towns and cities in Ontario and the W'est are going to continue to tas these properties and to obtain that revenue, that the same right should be given to New Brunswick and Nova Scotia.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speechtext: Certainly not. We have been negotiating for two years. We have refused the Grand Trunk's terms. If my hon. friend would only read the correspondence he would see that the Grand Trunk people have protested again and again and again against what it claims our unfair terms; it claims that we are not treating them fairly; that we are confiscating their stock. My hon. friend will note the agitation in the English press about the matter. In order to reach an understanding, because the situation had to be cleared up in some way, we offered in our letter of the 11th July, 1918, to treat this guaranteed stock in the same way as the debenture stock by our undertaking to pay interest upon it We undertook, in case of an arbitration, to do that, and after negotiating from July, 1918, until October, 1919, the Grand Trunk people finally have accepted that proposal, although during all that time they have been refusing to agree to it, because they thought it was putting them in an unfair position.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I do not think we shall make any headway by further discussing the point. My hon. friend's difficulty is this: He is not a lawyer; he does not draw-

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

He is not, I believe, accustomed to dealing with stocks and bonds in relation to corporation and finance, or he would clearly understand that the position he is taking is wholly untenable, and does not touch the question of public ownership at all. But I do not think we shall 
get any further ahead by any effort on my part to convince him that he is wrong, and my hon. friend will certainly not make any headway in endeavouring to convince me that he is right.

subtopic: BILL PROVIDING- FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

I should not
like to stand in the position of a legal expert for a moment, but I would be prepared to stand in the position of a man of average intelligence who is going to be held responsible for this agreement, when it is carried out, in the way of meeting its obligations, and it is to get an explanation that the average citizen will comprehend that I am putting these questions. Apart from legal phraseology and technicalities of one kind or another, I would ask the minister it what he has just told us does not amount to this, namely, that the Government of the day is negotiating with the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and that it cannot make certain terms because the Grand Trunk is not prepared to accept those terms. As I recall my hon. friend's question, it was this: Were the Grand Trunk Railway Company pressing to sell the system to the Government? That is my recollection of the question.

subtopic: BIDD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BIDD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
My answer to that is: No, the Grand Trunk Railway Company did not wish to sell; in fact, that was the last thing it wished to do. I might state in a few words the position taken by the company. What it wished was additional assistance from the Government for the Grand Trunk Pacific, such as it had been receiving in recent years, the Government advancing to the Grand Trunk Pacific a sum sufficient to enable it to practically pay its deficits and continue operation. The Grand Trunk Company pressed the Government to continue that assistance. The Government took the position that it would not be justified in continuing year after year to advance millions of dollars to assist this road, and that the people of Canada would not approve of its being done. The refusal to continue assistance to the Grand Trunk for the benefit of the Grand Trunk Pacific forced the situation which led to the receivership. The company said it did not have the money to continue operation of the Grand Trunk Pacific and therefore would be obliged to discontinue. It justified the claim for assistance on the ground, that when it undertook in 1903 and 1904 to build the Grand Trunk Pacific, it was to open up and develop a certain territory; that subsequent to that date the Government had given assistance, by way of guarantees, to the Canadian Northern railway to parallel the Grand Trunk Pacific line; that the result of the new construction thus started had greatly increased the cost of construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and at the same time had deprived it of traffic which otherwise would naturally have flowed to it ; and that it never would have undertaken to build the railway had it had any knowledge of the course that the Government subsequently pursued. Even on that ground the Government did not feel justified in making further advances. The Grand Trunk not only did not want to sell, but still declined the cash offer the Government made of $2,-$500,000 rental for the first three years,

$3,000,000 for the next four years, and $3,600,000 thereafter, insisting that that was wholly inadequate, and that it would be virtually confiscation to force it to accept that offer. Therefore the company finally accepted the alternative of arbitration.

subtopic: BIDD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: The question to which [DOT]ny lion, friend refers was partially as he states it. Let me put it in another form, however. It has been stated freely in this debate as the justification-that is the word my hon. friend would use; as the excuse, I would say-for the pressing forward of this matter at this time that it is one of great urgency. Now, my question, if I may repeat it, is this: Was that urgency on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway or on the part of the Government? My hon. friend talks of some negotiations that took place in connection with the receivership of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but that event happened many months ago and cannot have been the basis of the present proceeding. If the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada were coming to the Government and urging them to take over this road, surely we should have some evidence of it in the papers which the hon. gentleman brought down. The beginning of this whole transaction is the effort made by the Government to get possession of the Grand Trunk. There is nothing in this correspondence to show that there was any urgency on the part of the Grand Trunk, for the condition my hon. friend describes was a condition that existed many months ago. Suppose that the arrangement-I am putting the question I put at an earlier stage of the Rebate between my hon. friend and his colleagues and Sir Alfred Smithers had not been come to for a week later, until the understanding-I won't say engagement- that the Government had given the House as to prorogation had taken effect; suppose the House had been prorogued, and then the understanding had been come to between the Government and Sir Alfred Smithers, what would have happened? What distressing situation would have arisen if that had been the position instead of the one we have to-day?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BIDD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: My hon. friend is quite correct in saying that there is nothing in the correspondence indicating urgency from the standpoint of the Grand Trunk. The fact, however, is that the Grand Trunk was in need of additional assistance, and within the past six weeks the Government has had to render assistance to the Grand Trunk to prevent it getting into more serious default-not assistance to the extent of millions, but a few 'hundred thousand dollars. Therefore the situation to be faced is, whether the Government is to continue giving that assistance? If not, it must deal with the purchase at this time. Now, what my hon. friend says is correct. If an understanding had not been arrived at until after the House had risen, naturally the matter would have had to stand until the next session of Parliament.

subtopic: BIDD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: And what interest would have suffered?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BIDD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: This interest would have suffered: The Government could not have closed the agreement, because the Government did not feel justified in closing an agreement on so important a matter without the approval of Parliament. The Government, therefore, would have had to let the whole matter stand over. The position of the Government is-and we must deal fairly throughout^-that the Government does not believe it to be in the national interest that the Grand Trunk should dispose of its road to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company or to any other corporation allied with it. My hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) smiles, but it is not a matter of theory; it is a matter of fact. If we afe not prepared to permit the Grand Trunk to deaf with others, then when we come to an understanding with it, I cannot possibly see what excuse there is for delay in consummating it. What reason is there for delay? It has been before the country for nearly two years. Why should we not deal with it? That is one thing, I cannot understand.

subtopic: BIDD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext: I suggest the additional reason: That in operating the white elephant that was unloaded on the country under the policy of our friends opposite, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental, the country is losing enormous sums of money.

speechtext: My hon. friend must not ask the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) to concur in that, because the President of the Council has said, as I have said, that that arrangement was an excellent thing for the people of Canada. speechtext:

Mr. RICHARDSON [DOT] I must differ from my hon. friend.

speechtext:
The- President of the Council was a member of the Liberal party in good standing at that time, loyally supporting Sir Wilfrid Laurier and the whole of us; and although we differ in some respects to-day I know him too well to imagine that he will repudiate the stand that he took on that occasion.. However, that is only by the way.
It has been stated here day after day that this is a matter of urgency. I think a fair question to put is this: Is the urgency on the part of the Grand Trunk Railway Company, or is it on the part of the Government? Now, if the Grand Trunk Railway Company has been coming to the Government and pressing its demands on it, why in Heaven's name have we not the evidence of that in the correspondence? Why do we have to have my hon. friend saying to us, " Oh, well, the Grand Trunk was hard up; the Grand Trunk would have to do this and would have to do that and would have to do the other thing." The Grand Trunk is a big, well-organized' corporation, and if it made any urgent demand upon the Government surely the Government, as business men, were in a position to ask that this request be put in writing so that it would be in the record. But there is no evidence of urgency here; the plea of urgency put forward in this debate is absolutely unfounded so far as any evidence of it in the correspondence is concerned. The only urgency is with the Government of Canada. The Government- they will say, for good reasons; I am not assailing that-made up their mind that they wanted to grab the Grand Trunk Railway system, and they have been pushing the matter; now they come and say that it was an urgent case. The urgency was on their part, not on the part of the Grand Trunk.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BIDD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
I do not think that there is much to be gained by prolonging this discussion. I was a supporter of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and I believed that the building of the Grand Trunk Pacific was a good thing, but I always had some doubt as to the wisdom of the extension of the road to the East at such a cost to the Country. But let that go. What I did not approve of, what I do not now approve of and what
[Mi. Richardson.]
I think was a colossal blunder, was permitting the Canadian Northern to duplicate these lines as a transcontinental railway. I think that it was a mistaken policy to permit the extension of the Canadian Northern from Western to Eastern Canada, to guarantee its bonds and to commit the credit of Canada to two transcontinental railways. It duplicated lines unnecessarily; it depreciated the value of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, and it made it more difficult for that company to meet its obligations, and, on the other hand, it imposed immense obligations on the Canadian Northern. But we will gain nothing, as the member for Leeds (Sir Thomas White) said in his address on this Bill, by mutual recrimination with regard to the responsibility for the difficulties which exist in respect of the transportation systems of Canada. We cannot gain anything by doing that; the difficulties are here and we have to meet them.
Now, the Government of Canada believes that it is in the national interest to acquire the Grand Trunk Railway system. We do not offer any excuses for that; we say that the national interest demands it. Nobody on this side has said that there is urgency in the sense that we must proceed without due deliberation. My hon. friend has been told that he can have all the time he wishes to consider it; the Minister of the Interior has repeatedly said: " Stay as long as you like to consider it." But we can see no reason why the propolal which has been before the people for a year and a half and which is in a position to be consummated should not now be carried out with full legislative authority. I do not hesitate to say that one reason why we should not delay is'found in the fact that powerful interests in this country are opposed to the Government's acquiring this road and are seeking to organize opposition to our acquiring it.

subtopic: BIDD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
They are organizing it.
Mr. ROWELiL: Yes, and we should only be putting a further opportunity into their hand of defeating something that we believe _ to be vital in the public interest. The Government, with knowledge of the hostility that is being organized against that which js in the public interest, would have failed to do its duty had it not proceeded with all due expedition, at the same time giving full opportunity for discussion and consideration of this important matter.

subtopic: BIDD PROVIDING FOR THE ACQUISITION OF THE SYSTEM BY THE GOVERNMENT.
speechtext:
Translated into the
language of the man in the street, that means that the hon. gentleman is afraid of public opinion; he is afraid that if the Gov-

ernment do not rush this thing through this session there will he an organized effort to defeat him. If public opinion is so strongly in support of this measure, why does the President of the Council fear an organized effort to defeat it? The hon. gentleman's plea is a confession that he is afraid of public opinion and he is rushing this thing through Parliament avowedly with the purpose of preventing public opinion from being heard.
I agree with my hon. friend that there is nothing to be gained by recrimination over the history of the railway question. If my hon. friend will get possession of the Minister of the Railways when he comes in arid pound that thought into him he will be doing a good service. Did not the Minister of Railways last night spend half the evening in denouncing the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier's Government and stating all the awful things that happened to the Grand Trunk Pacific contract? My hon. friend says that a mistake was made in subsidizing the Canadian Northern alongside of-the Grand Trunk Pacific. There is some force in that argument, and I am always prepared to admit an argument made by an opponent when it has some weight. But he should point out also that while the Liberal Government subsidized and assisted that road, the Conservative Government carried it on right through to the coast. When the member for Leeds (Sir Thomas White) said- and I give him credit for it-that the credit or discredit, as the case may be, of this great railway enterprise, any mistakes made in connection with this great railway enterprise should not be ascribed to one party or the other; they should be distributed, over the two parties. In our zeal, having great faith in the future, we were, perhaps, too zealous to build ahead of the times. I have faith enough in the country to- believe that within the lives of the young men of this House, and of some who are no longer young, there will be a justification for these roads, and that in the building up of the country we shall have business enough for them all.
Cooning back to the question of urgency, again and again the statement is made that if we do not do this thing now some awful thing will happen. Is that an exaggeration? That is the substance of half the statements that have come from the other side. Mr. Chairman, I have been trying to find out what this awful thing is. My hon. friend says that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company will get possession of this system. Now, he knows that the Canadian Pacific
cannot get possession-I doubt whether they want to get possession of it, but that is their business-without coming to this Parliament. Then why should this bugaboo about the Canadian Pacific Railway be dragged into this transaction again and again?
Then, he says, if we do not allow the Canadian Pacific Railway to take it, we must take it ourselves. These are large questions for the future. Before this transaction goes through, all these accounts, the complicated accounts of the Grand Trunk Railway system should be examined-it would take a chartered accountant months to understand them. Subsidiary companies, connected interests in Canada and the United States, hotels, steamships, railways -there never was such a complicated transaction submitted to this House. Yet the hon. gentleman is rushing it through on the plea of urgency, and while the correspondence shows that the only people who are under the necessity of urgency are the Government, he is trying to grab this road and to put this thing through Parliament because he is afraid that public opinion will be against him.

speakeroldname: Hon. C. J. DOHERTY (Minister of Justice) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
That it is expedient that Parliament do approve of the Treaty of Peace between the Allied and Associated Powers and Austria, signed at St. Germain on the tenth day of September, one thousand nine hundred and nineteen, a copy of which has been laid before Parliament, and which was signed on behalf of His Majesty, acting for Canada by the plenipotentiaries therein named, and that this House do approve of the same.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it will be remembered that on the 22nd September, in answer to a question put as to the action contemplated by the Government with regard to the Treaty with Austria, it was stated that if a copy of the Treaty which had been signed arrived whilfe this House was still in session, the Treaty would be submitted to this House as was the Treaty with Germany. As the House is aware, the Treaty has been received and copies have been distributed and have been now for some days in the hands of members. This motion is intended to implement the promise so made. It is also within the recollection of the members of the House that, upon an amendment to the Bill coming before the House, giving powers to the Governor in Council to do those things which would be necessary for the carrying out of the Treaty with German^ and the giving effect to its provisions, which amendment was. made in the Senate and which extended the provisions of the Bill so as to include powers for the carrying out of the Treaty with Austria and the fulfilment of its provisions, this House accepted the amendment made, and included in that Bill, which, as I said, conferred the powers that I mentioned, the Treaty with Austria. For reasons which were then given, this House did not assent to the inclusion in that Bill of the conferring of powers in regard to treaties not signed and the giving effect to the provisions of such treaties. We have now before us, as I have said, the Treaty with Austria. As I pointed out when the amendment to which I referred was before the House, the Treaty with Austria, in all essential points, I think I might 
say in all points save where it deals with matters which are necessarily different in the two treaties, such as, for instance, the boundaries that require to be settled with regard to Germany in the one instance and with regard to Austria in the other, is identical in all respects upon lines absolutely similar, and practically with regard to all important measures, with the German Treaty. It was because of that fact that the Government felt justified in making the statement it did, that if the Treaty did not arrive while this House was in session, and if, iri consequence of the House not being in session, it would be impossible to submit it to the approval of the House except by calling a special session, the Government would be warranted, in view of the approval of the House given unanimously to the German Treaty, in advising the ratification of the Austrian Treaty without calling the House together again for that purpose. The Government arrived at that conclusion and made that declaration because, under those conditions, the approval of the German Treaty was naturally tantamount to an approval of the Austrian Treaty, and to have held up the latter Treaty under those circumstances merely until there would be an opportunity to submit that absolutely similar Treaty to the House, would have been holding up the Treaty for the purpose simiply of fulfilling a formality, the substance of approval having already in effect been given. I think I pointed that out at the time I had occasion to say what the Government desired to say with regard to the amendment made by the Senate. The adoption of that amendment, while in a sense it might be taken as implying approval of the Treaty, nevertheless had no further or greater effect than to confer upon the Government power to carry it out and to take such steps as might be necessary to give effect to its provisions. Before that power could come to be exercised at all, the Treaty would have to become binding upon Canada, and it would only have become so binding by reason of the ratification of His Majesty on the advice of the Government of Canada. The only circumstances in which the Government would have felt justified in ratifying the Treaty without special submission to Parliament would have consisted purely-and simply in the fact that in the case of the German Treaty, which in all important respects is identically the same as this Treaty, the Government had acted only after the express approval of this House with the text of the Treaty before them.

However, the Austrian Treaty has arrived and we have been in a position to lay it before the House, and there is now no occasion for the Government basing its action upon that which I have described as the substantial approval, the equivalent of the express approval, by this House of that particular Treaty. The Treaty is now before the House which by this motion is asked to express the same approval of it that the House unanimously expressed with regard to the Treaty with Germany. It is not necessary, I fancy, that I should this evening go into any explanation or exposition of the provisions of this Treaty. The House has had it in its possession for some days now, and I have no doubt that hon. gentlemen who have read it carefully have found that its text fully justifies what I pointed out in connection with the amendment to which I have already referred, namely, that the Treaty is in all important respects identical with, and in all matters substantially the same as, the German Treaty. Certainly it is on the same lines. So, without detaining the House further at the present moment, I ask the House to adopt the motion.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. D. McKENZIE (North Cape Breton and Victoria):
speechtext: I have very little to say upon the motion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty), because I think his motion and this whole proceeding puts this House in a very extraordinary and unusual position, to say the least. It is about a week or ten days ago since the minister came to this House with an amended Bill. An amendment had been made in the Senate in which the minister asked us to concur, the effect of such concurrence being to ratify this Treaty. Bill No. 3, which we passed this session dealing with the German Treaty, although it is word for word on exactly the same lines as the British Act ratifying the Treaty, did not express our approval or ratification of the Treaty. It was to implement the Treaty by furnishing the money that was necessary to carry out its terms, and to give the Government power to appoint the officials necessary to be appointed under the Treaty. The minister told us then, and quite properly so, that the passing of that Bill necessarily implied our approval of the Treaty.

The British Bill when
it passed the House of Commons in England implied, although it did not mention, approval of the Treaty, because it was for the purpose of furnishing the money for carrying out the terms of the Treaty, and of ,course if Parliament did not approve of the Treaty it would not furnish the means for carrying it out. Why, therefore, does the minister come here to-night and ask the House to go through the empty ceremony of re-approving something that has already been approved? I do not admit that there is any necessity for it at all. When we were dis-. cussing this matter ten days ago I read Lord Milner's despatch in this House, which, of course, had reached the minister long before we saw it. Lord Milner on the [DOT]advice of the law officers of the Crown in Great Britain advised the British Government that the approval of the British Parliament was not necessary, nor the approval of this Parliament. On the strength of that I argued that it was not necessary for us to do anything at all except what the British North America requires of us in order to furnish the wherewithal to carry out the Treaty so far as it imposed duties upon us. For that reason, although I am not going to offer any strenuous opposition, I think it would be more dignified for the House to stand by its action. We have already approved this Treaty, because we have passed an Act implementing it. I think it would be more consistent with the dignity of the House- although I suppose it does not in any way detract from our dignity to confirm our action, having done a thing once and believing we have done it right, and in fact

knowing it was right so far as its constitutionality and legality are concerned-to stand by our action of a week or so ago. I do not think we are adding any strength to our position by doing the thing over again in this way.

When the Minister
of Justice (Mr. Doherty) spoke of the careful consideration and reading which he was sure the members of the House had given to this document, I thought I observed a merry twinkle in his eye. Now I am going to make probably the risky statement that I doubt whether a single man in this House has read this interesting document of one hundred and fifty pages. It might be very wicked to suggest that the distinguished Canadian who signed it had not read it, but even that is a possibility. However, I believe the House is going to pay the Minister of Justice the high complement of approving this Treaty, not because they have ever read it, but simply upon his assurance that the Treaty is in all substantial things the same as the German Treaty. I confess I have not read it myself, but I am going to support the motion, simply on the faith that my hon. friend has spoken correctly in that respect.
It is a technical point, and I do not think of very much importance, but I observe that the resolution speaks of the Treaty being signed by the plenipotentiaries acting for Canada, whereas my hon. friend will see by looking at the Treaty that it is signed by only one plenipotentiary.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. H. SINCLAIR (Antigonish and Guysborough):
speechtext:
There is one point in connection with the Treaty in regard to which I should like to have an explanation from the Minister of Justice. Article 4 of the Covenant of the League of Nations, which 
is part of the Treaty, contains the following provision:
The Council shall consist of representatives of the principal Allied and Associated Powers, together with representatives of four other members of the League. The four members of the League shall be selected by the Assembly from time to time in its discretion. Until the appointment of the representatives of the four members of the League first selected by the Assembly, representatives of Belgium, Brazil, Spain and Greece shall be members of the Council.
On page 11 of the Covenant there are given the thirty-two original members of the League of Nations, who are signatories of the Treaty of Peace, and there is also a list of states invited to accede to the Covenant. In this list of nations that are not now members of the League, but who are to be invited to become members, we find Spain. Belgium is one of the original members of the League, and so is Greece; but Spain is not yet a member. How is it that Spain has representation on the Council when she is not a member of the League of Nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Nobody will have representation on the 'Council until the League of Nations is formed by the accepts ance and ratification of the Treaty, so far as the signatory nations are concerned. Spain will have representation on the League only after this has come about, and, of course, when she has accepted the invitation extended to her, and which- whether it was formally announced or not -the Conference, in accepting this Treaty, and the Commission in drafting it, were amply satisfied that Spain would accept. Nobody is a member of the LeagUe yet, because the League will come into existence only when the Treaty becomes effective. And it was in anticipation that, as soon as that should happen, Spain, availing herself of the invitation, would" become a member of the 'League, that all the nations signing this Treaty agreed that among the first four other members to be selected by the Assembly Spain should have representation upon the Council.
There are twenty-six nations who are already members of the League. Why select a nation not yet a member of the League and one that may never become a member?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I pointed out a moment ago that no nation will be a member of the League until the Treaty i.s ratified.
They are described as signatories.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are signatories of the Treaty and as such they become entitled to be members of the League. But the League is created by the Treaty.' The Covenant of the League is part of the Treaty and that part of the Treaty produces no more effect than any other part until the whole Treaty comes into force. When 'the whole Treaty becomes effective, that is to say, when it shall have been ratified by at least three of the great powers, then the provision which says that the signatories of the Treaty are members of the League will become effective with all the other provisions. As I pointed out, it was in anticipation of Spain's acceding to this particular part of the Treaty that the thirty-two signatories decided that it was proper to allow this representation to her. And, while I cannot say what were the motives of all those thirty-two nations, I believe it was considered desirable that at the initiation of the League the representation on its council should not be confined absolutely to the allied and associated powers. It was conceded as a courtesy, if you will, but at all events it was thought desirable, to include a nation which was not one of the allied or associated powers. I can only suggest that as being among the motives that may have impelled the thirty-two nations to that decision. Twenty-seven of those thirty-two nations being the nations who, when tbhe League would come into operation, would be entitled to elect the four other members, thought proper to include among the four one nation who would become a member by acceding to the Covenant, All of the nations are yet to become members, some merely by ratification of the Treaty, and others by acceptance of the invitation to come in, and it was in anticipation of their becoming members in one way or the other that the composition of the first council was decided upon.
