speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I rise, Mr. Speaker, simply to answer the question of my hon. friend in reference to the position of the International Labour Conference. That conference is officially called to meet on the 29th of this month-that is to say, on Wednesday next- at noon, in Washington, and it will meet pursuant to that call. But whether it will be able to proceed with the consideration of the matters mentioned in the agenda for the conference is a question which will not be known until the conference meets. So far as I am aware, the Treaty with Germany has not yet been ratified iby the three powers necessary to bring it into operation. The Treaty is not yet in effect. It may go into effect before the conference meets or on the following day. I have no knowledge ir^that respect other than the intimation, which appeared in' the press recently, that the Treaty was likely to he ratified and go into effect about that date. Notice has been issued iby the Secretary of Labour of the United States, intimating that it might be necessary to adjourn the conference in view of the fact that the United States had not-yet ratified the Treaty, and therefore was not in a position to take part in the conference.
Many of the delegates have arrived in the United States from foreign countries. I believe the British, the Spanish, and Japanese delegates, as well as the delegates from a number of other nations have already arrived in Washington for the work of the conference. It is a matter worthy of consideration that Canada takes part in the conference as one of the original members thereof and with the same status as all the other members of the conference. The Government in this case, pursuant to the provisions of the convention, has asked the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, as being the largest group of employers of labour in Canada, to name a delegate representing the employers, and has asked the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada, as being the largest organization representing organized labour, to name the labour representative to the conference. These bodies have named their representatives, and the advisers have also been named as

provided for under the terms of the convention.

When the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) ten days ago asked the House to concur in certain amendments to Bill No. 3 made by the Senate, he explained that he did so because it would make unnecessary the submission of the Austrian Treaty separately to the House. As I understood him at the time, and my understanding is confirmed by reference to Hansard, which under the rules of the House I believe I am not allowed to quote, that was the ground on which the House, at the hon. gentleman's request, concurred in these amendments. That being the case, I desire to know whether the proceeding which the hon. gentleman has submitted to the House by his motion is necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps I might state now if i't is in order-

Mr. Speaker, I did not anticipate that we should be asked this day to consider a matter the importance of which is as great as that of some of the measures which have been discussed within the last ten days in this Plouse. Had I expected that this question would be brought up this evening I should have prepared for the occasion. I find myself obliged to speak extemporaneously on a subject of international importance. We were called together at this time of the year to approve of the Peace Treaty and the League of Nations, on both of which I have already spokfen. Only to-day did I receive the blue-book on the subject of the Austrian Treaty, and by no means did I expect at this sitting of the House, when the representatives of the two adjacent provinces should be at home spending the week end, that this Treaty would be brought up for confirmation.
It is true that I am not a politician and I do not know all tihe devious ways by which the members of this Government may work to their ends, but that this Government should ratify, or confirm, or approve of the Austrian Treaty with the Allied Powers on the basis of what has already been said in the House with reference to the Treaty between the Allied Powers and Germany is difficult to understand. It is going absolutely too far because the conditions which obtain in one case are not the conditions that obtain in the other.
It is true that it is said by the Government in answer to a question by the Opposition, that what obtained in one case obtained in the other except as to terri-
[Kr. Rowell.]
torial limitation. I am not satisfied that that is correct because I have not had the opportunity to read the blue-book which was sent to. me through the mail to-day, and which I only received at three o'clock. But at any rate you have the question of Poland to consider in the Austrian Treaty, you have the question of Galicia to consider in the Treaty between Austria and the Allied Powers, you have many and varied questions. Is this Government so devoid of a sense of responsibility that it must, on a Friday evening, when there is not sufficient representation on the Opposition side or on the Government side, undertake to deal with a matter of international importance in this manner?
For instance, we have had questions put in this House by hon. members on this side of the House as to whether or not Poland guaranteed the liberty of the Ukran-ians in Galicia both as to their religion and as to their civil rights. We received the assurance from the members of the Government that these had been guaranteed. But it is only within the last few days that I had a message from certain Ukranians in the western provinces which I transferred to the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty). I understand from the Minister of Justice that a cablegram has been sent overseas dealing with this question but no answer has been received yet as far as I know. There is also the question as to whether or not the Ukrhnians in Galicia will be given a plebiscite
9 p.m. in order to determine whether they shall remain Poles or whether they shall remain Ukranians and form part of the great republic which has been already declared in the southern portion of Russia. We are now asked to ratify, confirm or approve of the Treaty between the Allied Powers and Austria. My hon. friend from George-Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) has repeatedly brought the question up in the House as to the foreign population in Canada-and let me tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I have absolutely no sympathy with the foreign population in Canada where they have shown no proper desire to serve their adopted country.
I am quite in sympathy -with the policy which has been enunciated by this Government, that that part of our foreign population which has not shown a desire to become assimilated should be deported. But there is also another policy which I believe in-the policy to conserve and improve that which we have acquired. This Government and its predecessors have spent thousands,

if not millions, of dollars to bring immigrants to our shores, and it is therefore the business of the Government of the day to see that these newcomers acquire our own ideas and become good Canadian citizens, rather than to talk of deporting them to their native land, where condition^ are worse than we have even thought of. Instead of presenting a Bill of this importance to a depleted House, I submit the Government should have deferred its consideration until the members absent over the weekend returned, in order that it might be thoroughly discussed.
Furthermore, in relation to Poland and Galicia, I wish to ask the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) if it is not true that during the war the Polish Council in Ontario had the ear and the confidence of this Government as to who should and who should not go overseas with our Expeditionary Force; if it is not true that this Government did receive the assistance of this Polish Council in that very regard; and if it is not true that this Government, while accepting the recommendations of this Polish Council, permitted it to take an affidavit from each and every individual who volunteered for service overseas that he owed fealty to Poland rather than to this country? What right has Poland to interfere in the business of Canada until the terms of the Treaty of Peace have been settled? What right had this Government to permit the Polish Counail in Ontario to take -affidavits of that character? There is no question, about that-it is true. I have seen the affidavits. I have also been requested to ask the Government whether or not this Polish Council was allowed to deal with Austrian cases, and I have submitted the whole matter to the Government. Why, for instance, should 80,000 Galician Jews now in this country be requested to swear that they are Poles, and threatened -that if they do not do so they will be deported or prosecuted? Why should Poland be given the right to dominate Galicia by simply declaring that the predominant element in the population is Polish?
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am quite willing to agree that Canada is not a nation. We have had a great deal of discussion on this point, which I do not intend to repeat, but no matter what may be the sophistical arguments advanced in favour of the contention that Canada is a nation, I assert that Canada is not a nation. In connection with any conference which may be convened in the near future with regard to preserving the peace of the world, I would ask any hon.
member this question: Does Canada represent any such principle of general interest as may compel the great powers of Europe -and the great power of America for that matter-to consider that we have a right to demand any particular remedy? If we are a nation then we must present a status of equality before the eyes of the world. This is denied us by the American nation; it is denied us by Britain; it is- denied us by France-in a word, it is denied us by all the associated powers who had anything to say in the Peace Conference, or who may have anything to say in the League of Nations. Why should we this evening, with so few members present, be called upon to approve a Treaty of Peace between Austria and the Allied Powers without taking into full consideration with those powers all the circumstances and all the facts of this Treaty? We talk about acquiring the Grand Trunk Pacific, we talk about prohibition and the transfer of Federal rights to the provinces -these are as nothing compared with what the Canadian nation is going to do as one of the groat world powers which are going to keep the peace upon earth. And yet I find myself suddenly confronted by a resolution of the Government brought forward at 9.15 on a Friday evening, when most of the Opposition members have gone to Quebec and Ontario over the week-end.
There is not much over there.

It is true that there is not much over there, I agree, both in the metaphorical and the literal sense; but there is less on this side-in both senses. I wish the co-operation of the House this evening in my request that this matter shall stand over until we have had an opportunity to study this Blue Book.
I have been flattered by the extent to which our chevelure has been ruffled with pride in the very thought that Canada shall take its place among the nations. It has been difficult for ne at times to comb my hair down in the mornings, with all the lotions that I like to apply, as I think of the tremendous position that Canada is to take among the nations of the world in preserving the peace of the world. But when we come down to actual facts-and I am making no academic speech this evening; I am speaking extemporaneously-we find difficulties for which we have not been prepared and it becomes necessary for us to protest, and I do so with all respect. I am a supporter of the Government-and may I always be permitted to support it rather

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I hope that the hon.
.member will bring his remarks to bear more closely on the subject that is before the House; he is going very far afield.

Mr. Speaker, I did not intend to go further away than I should go; I had intended from the reference which I made to draw a conclusion which would come more closely to the subject. However, I accede to your request, and say this: The resolution before the House is one that should receive the greatest possible consideration; one that is more important than *the passing of a Grand Trunk Railway Bill; one that is more important to the national life of this Dominion of Canada than any Bill that has been presented; and we are asked in the hours of a Friday evening to pass a matter which, if properly debated; should occupy several weeks, in order to ascertain the proper information upon which the conclusions' are reached in this resolution, in order to acertain the true state of affairs in Europe about which we are legislating, in order to ascertain how we, as a nation or a colony, are responsible for the terms of these things about which we are to legislate. If these are not more important than free trade; if these are not conditions more important than any other matter that has been before the House, I say that we are not paying very much regard to the consequences of those things upon which we are legislating. It is simple, to pass an Act; it is simple to vote upon a resolution; but it is not simple to accept the consequence of our own acts; it is not simple-and I hope I am not wandering far away from the resolution now-that we, as a Canadian people, as a part of the League of Nations, should accept the responsibilities of what may be the voting power within the League of Nations. It is not material to you, Sir, and to me, whether you, I, your children or mine, shall participate in the future wars of this world without being consulted, simiply on the declaration that "when Great Britain is at war we are at war/' It is not material to you or to me that we should accept all our share of responsibility of what is being done by the League of Nations without having had a voice in the matter or having been consulted. That is what we are doing in this resolution when we approve the terms of this Treaty, without knowing what are the particulars of the Bill or the -menu which we are ordering. These are things about w'hich I have a concern. It may be very simple for the Minister of Justice, or the Minister of Customs, or the Minister of Public Works now to say in the House: We have gone; we have come; we have conquered; or we came, we saw and we conquered. It is f very simple thing for these hon. gentlemen paid by the Canadian nation, to perform a duty towards the whole Empire, towards the whole world, to come back and say: This is what we have done. We are entitled to ask them for a bill of particulars. When I was a student at McGill university, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) lectured to me on marriage covenants,	I took	heed:	of what hetold	me in	those	days, and I
have been true to the lessons that he gave me. It is true that I am not going to confess to him all my weaknesses, but what he fold me in regard to marriage contracts I have followed religiously in giving advice to others, for which advice I have been paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The hon. member should give me a commission.

But I do not accept the dictation of the Minister of Justice as an envoy of the Canadian nation to deal for me in the problems of the world unless he is prepared to show to me that the law that he hands down to me is well founded upon certain commandments or until such time as I find his reasoning is in accordance with the exigencies of the case.
Carried.

I am very glad that this note of warning comes from the Opposition. I have sat on this side of the House when I have felt in my heart I should shout "carried." I have been sick at hear often times when the Opposition have started, and before they have gone but a few minutes, I have felt that I should have liked to cry " carried." If they are sickened as much as I have been at times of their oratory, I shall be pleased to take my seat.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before the Minister of
Justice exercises his right to reply,I wish to remind hon. members that if any hon. members desire to speak, they should do so now; otherwise, the debate will be closed.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I find myself in a
somewhat embarrassing position. Whereas I have to meet, coming from in front of me, the reproach that I am asking this House merely to do what it has already

done, and that, therefore, my proceeding is absolutely futile, there comes from behind me a very grave arraignment for that I am asking the House, without proper information, and saddest of all on a Friday night, to pass this most important resolution. May I point out, to deal first with the observations of the hon. member (Mr. H. A. Mackie), that he in common with all the members of this House has already expressed approval of those provisions which, if I have followed his arguments of this evening, give rise to most doubt and most desire for information, and indeed in some cases to direct opposition on his part. The hon. gentleman spoke of Poland and objected to our expressing approval of this Treaty until we had further explanations with regard to conditions in that country. May I just point out to him that in this particular	Treaty, the	one
reference to Poland is that Austria says that she accepts the boundaries of Poland as already fixed by the Allied and Associated Powers; that is to say, the boundaries were fixed in the Treaty with Germany which the hon. gentleman has already approved. Furthermore, with regard to his observations in connection with the protection of the rights of minorities in Poland, may I point out to him that he has already approved the Treaty with Poland which has been submitted to this House and in which it is expressly stipulated that Poland shall respect all those very rights to which he has so eloquently referred. With regard to his reference to the Ukrainians, there is nothing in this Treaty that bears upon the provisions in regard to the Ukrainians and more particularly upon what questions may arise between certain Ukrainians, native or former inhabitants, I believe, of Galicia and Poland, and this simply because, as I have said, it is in the other Treaty with which we have already dealt that the boundaries of Poland are fixed, and because we have dealt with a special Treaty which imposes upon Poland that she shall respect the rights of minorities of all classes.
As to the Ukrainians to whom the hon. gentleman refers and in connection with whom-I do not think the matter was very relevant-he arraigns this Government for the line of action it has seen fit to adopt in the past in connection with certain Poles as also in connection with certain Ukrainians in this country, let me very briefly state just exactly what the situation is. The hon. gentleman has referred to a Council of Poles whom he says this Govern-

ment have recognized and upon whom he seems to conceive that this Government has conferred some power or authority to compel Ukrainians to swear that they are Poles. The situation with regard to that Council is a very simple one indeed. Poles are nationals of an allied power. We had certain restrictions in this country as to freedom of departure from Canada imposed upon alien enemies, and when people came forward and said that they were Poles we found that it was of advantage in the absence of any particular Polish consulate or consul to be able to have their claims verified by people known to be of that nation and in a position to vertify' whether they were Poles or not, and we did accept from persons claiming to be Poles, as part of the evidence going to establish that claim -not, however, without further verification in cases where it was called for,-the certificates of this Council to persons known to be Poles and respectable and reliable people. I understand that the complaint of the Ukrainians which the hon. gentleman has voiced has been that they were compelled to swear they were Poles. Now it is only natural that when they went to that Polish Council asking for certificates the Council would say to them "The thing that we undertake to certify is that a man is a Pole or not a Pole. If you are not a Pole we have nothing to do with you." I do not know that they required them all to swear they were Poles, but if they did, it was perhaps not an unnatural thing for a body called upon to certify that a certain individual was a Pole to ask him whether he was willing to swear that he was a Pole.
What I said was that they were called upon not to swear that they were Poles, but to swear fealty to Poland.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the hon. gentleman will find himself mistaken in that regard, although I do not say that positively. I do not think it involved the question of swearing allegiance to anybody. Certainly the only question in which we were interested and which could have any relation with that Council was whether the .particular individual was a Pole or not. It may be-I am not prepared to say it was not so-that in the process of testing whether a man claiming to be a Pole really was a Pole-and he had no business going to the Council unless he was representing he was a Pole-they called upon him to swear fealty to Poland. Some of these people, and I have had representations from

different ones, seem to have misunderstood the situation, and to have
supposed that in order to get out of Canada they were having imposed upon them through some sort of governmental authority an obligation to say they were Poles. I have explained just to what extent we were interested in the question whether they were Poles or not, and it was not with any idea of inducing people to swear they were Poles so that they might on false representation get out of the country that anybody would have been asked to make an affidavit. There was a misapprehension on the part of these people who do not readily grasp and understand-and quite naturally-the different regulations to which they were subjected.
I may say that on the part of this Government there has been a desire to afford Ukranians who are individually responsible and reliable people and not subject to deportation every means that can be found of enabling them to establish those facts. There certainly has been no desire to discriminate against the Ukrainians. There exists at the present time in the city of Montreal a Ukrainian body to whose certificates with regard to persons claiming to be Ukranians in connection with their respectability and fitness to be allowed to remain in the country great weight is attached by the officers of this Government. Let me assure the hon. gentleman, who, I know, takes great interest in the people of this race, that there is no desire on the part of this Government to discriminate in any way against these people. Of course, for the purpose of assuring ourselves of proper control of persons of alien enemy races within this country it was unavoidable that these people, being, as they were during the course of the war nationals of an enemy country, should be subjected to regulations, but I am quite certain that on the part of this Government in the administration of tnose regulations both towards Ukranians and people of other races there was no desire to do any injustice or act with any harshness.
With regard to the observations in connection with the treaty which the hon. gentleman made, I think I am safe in saying that the different matters that he adverted to are all of them matters which were covered by the provisions of the treaty with Germany, and he is not being asked, in regard to any matters so far as 1 can recall them to which he referred, to approve of anything which he has not already approved in approving the German Treaty. He spoke of
the obligations of the League of Nations. Let me point out that this Parliament has approved the Covenant of the League of Nations as contained in the German Treaty, and we are not binding ourselves any more now because the Covenant is also found in the Austrian Treaty. It is just the same Covenant, and whatever may be the extent of its obligations we have already assumed them in approving the German Treaty. I feel that I have not taken up seriatim, and very possibly have not done full justice to all the representations made by the hon. gentleman. But I have endeavoured to meet them in a general way at all events, and if I have overlooked any of them I trust he will not consider that it was because of any intentional discourtesy on my part. I would be quite incapable of that. I am very touched by his assurance of his recollection and appreciation of valuable lessons which in earlier days it was my privilege to address to him.
With regard to the question of the hon. member for Russell (Mr. Murphy) and some observations made by hon. gentlemen opposite, rather reflecting upon the utility of the present proceedings, I am free to admit that perhaps this is not absolutely necessary, but the other day in connection with the amendment which I moved that this House should accept, there was a good deal of criticism, and it was pointed out that it was not absolutely regular, which I concede, to ask the House to confer t'he powers that were conferred by that amendment, the House not having before it the actual text of the treaty. I think I acknowledged then that it would have been better if the text of the treaty had been before the House, and I supported the suggestion that we accept the amendment upon what seemed to me to be the common sense ground, namely, as the House had already-expressed its approval, in the form of the Treaty with Germany, of all the substantial provisions of this treaty, that, subject to the House being willing to accept the assurance of the Government that this Treaty was similar, it would be a comimonsense action on tlhe part of a body in that situation, having conferred the powers upon the Governor in Council necessary for the implementing of the German Treaty, to consent to confer the same powers, in so far as they might 'be required, for the purpose of implementing and carrying out the Austrian Treaty. And, if my memory serves me, I pointed out that that legislation would never come into practical operation, unless the Treaty with

Austria became binding by its ratification. I then called attention to the assurance *which had already been given to the House by the Government, that it would only advise that ratification without coming back to this House if the Treaty, when it reached us, proved to be so identical with the German Treaty that you could not escape the conclusion that a House that had approved the provisions ^contained in the German Treaty would, consistently with itself, approve the provisions contained in the Austrian- Treaty.
But, fortunately or unfortunately, the session has been prolonged until the Treaty has reached us, and now we put it before the House. It was suggested then that there was something irregular in our not having it before the House. Now we have met that suggestion and have put it before the House, and asked the House to approve it. We do that to meet the suggestions I refer to, and to carry out the promise made on the 22nd of September that it would be done. After all, is it a very grave ground of complaint that we should seek, if you will, to make assurance doubly sure? If we have already, in passing the amendment referred to, approved this Treaty, it can do no possible harm that we should now do it formally and precisely with the Treaty before us, if for no other reason than that we should have the approval of the Treaty absolutely regular in .form, although the approval of the German. Treaty is substantially the approval of the Austrian Treaty.

Will the minister permit me two questions? Will Poland allow the Ukrainians in Galicia to determine whether or not they shall remain part of Poland or become part of the Ukrainian Republic? Secondly, when was the Treaty of Peace between the Allied and Associated Powers and Austria signed? Was it on the 10th day of September, 1919, and was a copy submitted to this Parliament? Further what opportunity has this House had of considering the same?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
With regard to what
Poland may do or may be compelled to do in connection with the position of the Ukrainians in Galicia, I may point out again that the question does not arise under the present Treaty with Austria, and perhaps, if the hon. member will reflect a moment, he will realize why. It is a question between the Ukrainian population of Galicia, and Poland; it is not a question between Austria and the Allied and Associated Powers. As to whether or not the 
Ukrainian population of that portion of Galicia which is claimed by, if not allotted to, Poland, in the boundaries fixed in the German Treaty, will be entitled to a plebiscite to determine their allegiance, is a question which, so far as my information at the present time goes, is not yet determined. It is still pending before the Council. As to the question when the copies of the Treaty were distributed, if I am correctly informed, the Treaty was laid on the table of this House some four days ago. I understood that the Treaty was to be distributed yesterday, but the particular hour at which it reached the members I am not prepared to say.
Three o'clock this afternoon. Now, may I ask another question, or at least, may I be permitted to correct an impression which has been given to the House by the minister?

speechtext:
The hon. member will

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
House again in Committee on Bill No. 31 to amend the Civil Service Act, 1918, with respect to the salaries of certain postmasters and assistant postmasters.-Hon. A.
K.	Maclean.-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-revenue from war stamps not to be included in postage collections when determining salaries of city and assistant city postmasters:

subtopic: SALARIES OF POSTMASTERS AND ASSISTANT POSTMASTERS.
speechtext: What is this?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SALARIES OF POSTMASTERS AND ASSISTANT POSTMASTERS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend (Mr. A.
K. Maclean) gave a very full explanation on -the second reading of the Bill. I _ can give any further information that is desired. The object of the Bill is to continue the right which has been given under certain Orders in Council, passed under the War Measures Act, to exclude from the salaries of city postmasters who are entitled to be paid a percentage of the receipts from the sale of stamps, the additional amount which it is figured they would have received on account of the war stamp tax. If they *sold a two cent stamp before they now sell a three cent stamp; if they sold a one cent stamp before they now sell a two cent stamp. It was not considered just that the salary should be increased by the percentage derived from the sale of 'stamps the proceeds of which were intended purely for war purposes. This has been in force since the War Measures Act was passed, and by Order in Council, and it is simply to continue it.

subtopic: SALARIES OF POSTMASTERS AND ASSISTANT POSTMASTERS.
speechtext:
One difficulty about
this is that it is practically impossible to carry it out except by sheer guesswork. It is not desirable to be dealing with a man's property by guesswork. The salary that a man earns by selling postage stamps and attending to his business in the post office is his property just as much as his house or his horse, and it is a part of the constitution-too old indeed to be mentioning it now-that no British subject shall be affected in his property or rights of any kind except by due process in a court of law. This salary which he earns is his property. We are going to pass an arbitrary Act in this Parliament, which is not a court of law in which this man can give evidence and with no machinery provided to enable him to give any explanation or testimony about his rights in this matter', authorizing some person to say "This is all you are to have; the rest of your earnings go to the Crown." I think this is a most

arbitrary piece of legislation. Besides, it is extremely difficult to know where the line *should be drawn. It was suggested at the time this law came into force that there should be a special stamp for war purposes and ordinary stamps for ordinary postal purposes. It was promised at that time that if we would agree to allow the ordinary stamps to be used promiscuously a special stamp would be provided. But things went on and it was never done; the postage stamps were used for other purposes. I think that it is better in the interest of fair play and in the interest of the country that things should be left as they are. If postmasters, by reason of this laxity got a few dollars extra-it will not be very much -I do not think it is woyth
10 p.m. while to create many sore hearts, a great deal of disappointment and irritation by starting out now to correct what was possibly a mistake. Take the case of the banks; they buy an enormous number of stamps. The banks use a great many postage stamps in their ordinary business. They have to use stamps on all their cheques, notes and drafts. They buy these stamps hut the post office does not lose the two cents nor do the banks; the- man who cashes the cheque pays for the two cents stamp. The postmaster sells these stamps, but how is anybody going to tell how many stamps went on bills, notes and cheques and how many were used in the hank for ordinary mailing purposes? It is absolutely impossible; there is no account kept. A sheet of stamps comes into the bank and these stamps -are used right and left as they are required. There is no attempt made to discriminate between those that go on letters and those that go on the cheques that are cashed for the customers of the bank.
Those are the reasons why I think the President of the 'Council (Mr. Rowell) and thb Government should test it before imposing this power and duty-which I am sure no one wants-upon any one to divide this money equitably between the Government and the postmasters. Therefore I think it would be very much better to leave matters as they are rather than bother with this legislation.
Mr. McQUARRIE': I was under the impression that this Bill would not come up until next week; in fact, I was so informed by the minister (Mr. Maclean) who was originally in charge of it.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SALARIES OF POSTMASTERS AND ASSISTANT POSTMASTERS.
speechtext:
If either the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) or I had been aware

of that understanding we would not have taken action. We are endeavouring to dispose of as many Bills to-night as possible. If there is any understanding with the minister (Mr. Maclean) that the Bill should stand over, of course, I do not wish to proceed with it.

subtopic: SALARIES OF POSTMASTERS AND ASSISTANT POSTMASTERS.
speechtext: He told me that it would not be proceeded with until he came back. I had some further remarks which I would like to make in connection with the Bill, but I do not care to deal with the matter when he is not here. For instance, he promised to give me information in reply to certain questions which I was not permitted to ask on the second reading. I presume that when he is here he will be prepared to give me that information.

subtopic: SALARIES OF POSTMASTERS AND ASSISTANT POSTMASTERS.
speechtext: Is the Bill intended to be retroactive? '

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: SALARIES OF POSTMASTERS AND ASSISTANT POSTMASTERS.
speechtext:
No. This is the present situation, regarding which my hon. friend the member for :Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) is under some slight misapprehension. The Government did pass an Order in Council under the War Measures Act fixing the percentage which should be considered as the proceeds of the war stamps from which the postmasters should not receive any return-my recollection is that it was 28 per cent, but I speak subject to correction-and that their salary should be computed on the basis of 72 per cent. As I understand it, the department in fixing that 28 per cent made the best estimate that was possible. Of course, I agree with my hon. friend that you cannot fix the percentage with	exactitude;	but I
am quite sure that the Post Office Department thought that in the percentage they fixed they were not taking any advantage of the postmasters, but were giving them the full measure of the proceeds of sale so far as the former postage would apply. My hon. friend will see that on three-cent stamps it would be a third, on two-cent stamps a half, and on war stamps the whole amount. Now, the object of this Bill is simply to continue in the Postmaster General the power to do what has been done until the new classification under the Civil Service Act goes into effect in April, 1920, when the scale of payment is fixed on a different basis.
With reference to my hon. friend from New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie), if he would discuss his point on the third reading, it would enable us to advance the Bill a stage; but in view of his understanding

with the minister I certainly shall not press on the Bill now.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext:
Clause 1 of the Bill
as reported by the special committee reads as follows:
1. The House of Commons Act, Revised Statutes of Canada, 1906, Chapter 11, is amended by inserting the following sections immediately after section eleven :-
11 A. In the event of a vacancy occurring by reason of the death of any member or by reason of his accepting any office a writ shall be issued within six months after the receipt by the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery of the warrant for the issue of a new writ for the election of a member of the House of Commons.
Provided, however, that this section shall not apply where the vacancy in respect of which the warrant has issued occurs within six months of the expiry of the time limited for the duration of the House of Commons, or if Parliament is dissolved after the issue of a new writ hereunder such writ shall thereupon be deemed to have been superseded and withdrawn.
11B. No person shall be eligible as a candidate for election as a member of the House of Commons in more than one electoral district at the same time, and no person shall be nominated or consent to be nominated so as to be a candidate for more than one electoral district at the same time, and if any'person is so nominated for more than one electoral district and consents thereto all such nominations shall be null and void.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: Is it the intention of this Bill that if a man is nominated in two places both nominations shall be void?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext:
The intention is that .all nominations consented to by the nominee, wherever a man is nominated for more than one constituency, shall be void. If a gentleman, by consenting to be nominated in two places, seeks to obtain a nomination which under this law would be illegal, both nominations shall be void. Of course, generally speaking, nominations without the consent of the candidate are void for want of that consent. But there is an amendment which I desire to suggest to 11B, and which has been accepted by the member (Mr. Jacobs) who introduced the Bill. I move to amend paragraph 11B by striking out all the words preceding the words "ne person " in the third line thereof and by substituting the word "and" for the word "or" in the fourth line. It did not seem fair that a man's absence, he being not in a position to control the thing, his election should be rendered impossible simply because he was nominated in .two places. It was pointed out to me-in my innocence I would never have thought of it-that if the nomination of a man in two places made

all nominations void his friends and supporters might nominate him in a constituency in which they bad every expectation that he would be elected and his opponents could prevent his even having a chance of being elected organizing to get somebody to nominate him in some other constituency. That is a possibility which, I think, should not be created. In the certainly exceptional case where it will happen both that a man is absent from the country and that he is nominated in more than one constituency, he may be elected for more than one constituency. If that does happen, the case is covered by the present provision of the law requiring him to make option, because that provision is not repealed. It is in order to avoid t.he possibility of an absent man being absolutely debarred from election by the mere fact of his absence and of his bein'g nominated in more than one. place unknown to himself that I have moved to strike out these words:
No person shall he eligible as a candidate in more than one electoral district at the same time.
Then the section goes on to provide that where nomination is made and consented to by any person for more than one place, all such nominations shall be void. But the effect of the first words which I have moved to strike out is, without reference to whether the person consents or does not consent, without reference to whether he is absent or present, to declare a person absolutely ineligible as a candidate-not ineligible as a member, hut even as a candidate-in more than one electoral district at the same time; the mere fact of nomination for two places would, therefore, render a man ineligible as a candidate in either. It did seem to me, and the member for George Etienne Cartier quite agreed with me, that that would be a desirable result to produce. But the great bulk of cases are the cases of men who are at home and whose consent is necessary to their nomination; and with regard to them we shall be ensuring that in the future no man will be elected for more than one constituency.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: In the case of nominations of that exceptional character to which the minister has referred, owing to the absence of the candidate, two nominations might be legal?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext:
I should be glad to devise a law that it would be impossible to evade. At all events, I think the effect of this law will be to reduce to the lowest possible degree the probability of our having people elected for more than one constituency. The men who are likely'to be nominated for more than one constituency are usually men of prominence in one or the other of the two great parties, men who would not care or who would not think it necessary to run away from the country for that purpose; while such an evasion is possible, 1^ confess that I cannot devise a method of rendering this law absolutely iron-clad.
I may say that the Solicitor General and myself gave some considerable time to trying to devise a system that would be absolutely perfect and render evasions impossible, and I am assured that the 'Committee on Privileges and Elections likewise devoted considerable time to the same purpose, but that they arrived at the conclusion that they could not find a way to make it an absolute certainty that nobody would ever he elected for more than one constituency. This provision, so far -as it goes, diminishes very materially the probability of that happening, and it is, so far as it goes, a distinct improvement to the law. Possibly as time goes on somebody may discover a method of further extending it so as to make it absolutely proof against evasion.

speechtext:
Not having before me a
copy of the Bill as amended, what I may have to say may be irrelevant; but dealing with the point which the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has

raised, that a man has only to leave the country to make himself eligible for two or more nominations, could not that ibe rectified by providing that he shall he held to he nominated in that constituency which stands in the highest alphabetical order, and that, say twenty-four hours being allowed, his other nomination shall be dropped; that he shall he considered not legally nominated in any of the others?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: The effect of doing that would be to assure to that man who went out of the country for the purpose that he would be nominated in at least one constituency. It would be a better way to deal with the matter, if that were a practical way, by some provision that if any person leaves the country for that purpose, his nomination shall foe void, but I realize the difficulty of making proof of that. It is true that we might do what the hon. gentleman suggests; tout if we did it, we would be depriving a constituency of the privilege of nominating a man who might foe bona fide absent. If we provided that where a man being absent is nominated for more than one constituency, his nomination shall stand good in that which is in the highest alphabetical order, all that his opponents will have to do when they find out that he is going to be nominated in a constituency that begins with " Z" will be to nominate him in another constituency the name of which begins with a higher letter and in which they know for an absolute certainty that he has not a gfoost of a chance of toeing elected. Then, if we adopt the amendment suggested, he will be a candidate in that place that begins with the highest alphabetical letter, and he will be effectively and assuredly defeated. I realize that it will still be possible under this measure, toy people who are willing to resort to contrivances of that kind, that a man may worm himself into two seats in this House, but it will not be as it is to-day with the door wide open for any man who wants to take the chances and who can get twenty-five people in each of two constituencies to nominate him, to try to get into the House. I think the (hon, gentleman will realize the force of what I point out, that if you choose a constituency for that man, you make it possible for his adversaries to select that constituency for him.

I am finding it very hard to understand just where we are at now. All that there iss. for the convenience of the members is the Bill as originally drafted, and this Bill has been amended in such a 87
way that clause 1 as originally drafted has been practically all changed. I understand that the Minister of Justice has moved an amendment to that clause as amended. Personally I have only a vague understanding of the Bill. No Ihon. member can reasonably (be expected to carry the terms of this Bill in his memory. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: The Bill is really hot a Government measure, and it is not in my charge. I am endeavouring to put it through this evening because the Bill as amended seems to be a very desirable measure and because I had agreed with the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier that he would have an opportunity of passing it. Hon, gentlemen may remember that at one time in the early part of the session there was an adjournment of the debate, and I think some hon. gentlemen were good enough to take it for granted that there was some desire because of that to shelve the Bill. On the contrary, the principle that underlies the Bill seemed to myself and the Government to be sound, and we were desirous that, subject to its being amended in certain details, it should have an opportunity of passing, and that is the reason why I am endeavouring to pass it now that an opportunity presents ltsell. As to the hon. gentleman fully grasping it, the measure coming before us as amended is reduced to such very small compass and is in the terms so little difficult of comprehension that if the Chairman would be good enough to read the Bill, I think the hon. gentleman would follow it without difficulty.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext:
Before the Bill is read for the information of members, I am afraid that this taking away the right of running m more than one constituency is going to create a good deal of trouble. As the election laws .stand now, there is no provision for the holding of a poll until two contending parties are nominated, and then there is a poll. Supposing, for instance, that two nominations are made in violation of this measure. They are two illegal nominations. One constituency does not know that the man is nominated elsewhere, perhaps a hundred miles away and both elections are held. The election of the man who has put in his nominations



improperly is void; he was never nominated. But supposing that in both cases he is defeated, it strikes me as a nice question of law if the other man is elected at all even if he gets a majority of votes, because it is perhaps an illegal poll where there was only one legal nomination.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext:
The reason why it would be an illegal poll, if it really were so held, would be that only one man. had been legally and regularly nominated and that there should not have been a poll at all; but the consequence of the fact that there should not have been a poll at all is that the ope man, being the only man legally nominated, would be declared elected.
So you have no complication in the case where it is the adversary of the illegally nominated man who is declared elected. You have, of course, the unfortunate circumstance that an expensive election has been held when it was not necessary. Might I ask the hon. gentleman, does he think it is a probable thing in Canada, does he even think it is a possible thing, that a man should be nominated in two constituencies and that the election should go on and that in those two constituencies nobody should know that that man was nominated in another constituency? Really, it seems to me hardly .possible. At election time our newspapers from one end of the country to the other contain lists the day after nomination of the people nominated in all the constituencies. After all, during an election people are pretty alert to ascertain who is the man that has been nominated on the other side, and I do not think we are running a very serious risk that elections will go on with a man nominated for more than one constituency and that the two constituencies for which he is standing will be quite ignorant of that fact, and will go on and hold the election and vote for the man who is nominated in both places. It might happen, but I think we would all be very much surprised if it did.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext:
If there is only one
person nominated the returning officer can declare him elected. If two men are nominated, one of them illegally and the other properly, he declares a poll; that is his duty. He cannot recall anything he has done and the election goes on. An hour after he has declared a poll he may discover that one of the candidates has been illegally nominated and that he never should have declared a poll, but he is absolutely powerless. He cannot declare that the candidate is elected any more than he can recall his having granted a poll. There is 
no machinery, so far as I know, to declare the man elected who was legally nominated and who received the majority of the votes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: I have not the statute before me, but I am inclined to think the hon. gentleman is right in his suggestion that there is no provision for declaring the man legally nominated in such a case to have been elected, but I think I can say without hesitation that in a case of that kind it would be perfectly possible for the man who was the only one legally nominated, if he would take the pains, to give the necessary publicity to the fact of the illegality and nullity of the other man's nomination to claim the seat, whatever was the result of the voting.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext:
That would have to be by petition.
' Mr. DOHIERTY: Yes. But if the man legally nominated got the majority of votes,
I do not think anybody would make a petition to unseat him on the ground that the votes given for him were not regularly taken because of the fact that his adversary was not regularly nominated. I think a man who came petitioning on that ground would be asked at the very threshold "What is your grievance? Do you who were illegally nominated feel aggrieved because the only man legally nominated has been declared to have a majority of the votes?" The legally nominated man would be doubly entitled to the seat in such a case. He would be entitled to it because he was the only legally nominated man, though the returning officer was not in a position to declare'it; but the court would be in a position to declare it.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext:
I would be very sorry to put a man to that trouble.
Mr. DOHERTYI doubt if there is anybody who would be willing to deposit $1,000 as security for an election petition the foundation whereof was that he or the candidate whom he supported, and for whose failure to be elected he is aggrieved, never had the right to be voted for at all. If anybody is so foolish as to spend $1,000 in support of a petition based on those grounds I think it would be a good thing for the gentleman who happened to defend the man declared elected, because he would have security for the costs and would get^ them paid, and would have no difficulty in defending the seat. I do not think there is much danger of anybody launching a contestation on that ground.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: I see that the provision with regard to the six months does not apply when a member resigns his seat, but only in the case of his death or acceptance of an office of emolument under the Crown.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: I understand that the reason which led the committee to exclude that case was that in their judgment it was not desirable that an individual member should have it in his power to force an election in his particular constituency at any time that he might feel like having it done. The purpose of the provision is to withdraw from the Governor in Council the power which, I think, from time immemorial he has enjoyed of fixing, or failing to fix, the date of an election when vacancies occur. I think there have sometimes been, perhaps under all governments, what might be described as abuses of that power, too long a period being .allowed to elapse without the writ being issued. The clause as reported by the committee provides that in cases other than those mentioned there shall be an absolute time limit within which the writ must be issued. In the judgment of the committee it was thought desirable not to put in the hands of every member representing a constituency the opportunity of forcing an election in that constituency at any moment he might think was a good time to bring on that election. If he thinks he ought to resign he is free to resign, but he ought not by his resignation to be able to determine that there shall be a new election in that constituency within a period fixed by statute, whether the public interest be or be nbt served by holding the election at that particular time.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: If a member were appointed to an office under the Crown and the Government did not want a by-election to be held in his constituency, he could resign before accepting the office, and then the seat would become vacant by resignation and not by acceptance of office.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: It would, of course, be a case of vacancy by resignation and this would not apply. That is apparently true. I suppose it is another case where improvement is possible, although we have improved the law.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: In the case of'a member resigning, the law would be as at present.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext:
It would be in the hands of the Government to determine, and I can see some force in the remarks of my hon. friend (Mr. Proulx). It is not unreason-

able to say that a constituency should not be deprived of representation for more than six months, no matter how the vacancy occurs. It is not the interest of the individual but of the constituency, and if we provide that the constituency may remain unrepresented for more than six months we are not making much of an improvement in the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: We are making an improvement to this extent, that whereas today the period may be indefinite we have now reduced it to a space of six months, not, of course, in the case where a member chooses to resign. Matters will be no worse in that case than they are under the present law. Lhey are not improved; that is to be conceded. I was not a member of the committee that considered this Bill and I do not feel authorized to do more than ask this committee to accept it as it was sent to us. It is true that I did move one amendment, but that was as a result of consultation with the hon. member who introduced the Bill, and with his assent. I would not like to try to extend its provisions further than the committee, with the assent of the hon. gentleman who introduced the Bill, thought proper to go.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: I quite appreciate my hon. friend's point in that respect, and I would not like to see the Bill adversely dealt with in the absence of the member who introduced it. But on the particular point to which attention was directed a moment ago, the Bill is open to objection. What seems to have been in the mind of the Committee was entirely the convenience or the possible aims of the individual. But it is a very grave error to exclude a constituency from representation in Parliament for a period , of six months or longer, and leave the matter entirely at the dictation of the Government of the day. 1 share my hon. friend's aversion to changing the Bill in the absence of the member who introduced it, and I think it might remain in committee.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: At the present time there is a by-election in Assiniboia as a consequence of a vacancy which occurred through a mem, ber resigning nearly two years ago. That constituency has been without representation for a period now of * nearly two years, the Government not having chosen to give the constituents an opportunity to return a member to Parliament. This Act would not alter that condition and would still leave it to the Government to adopt a similar course.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext:
In the particular instance the vacancy was attributable, I

think, to the fact that the gentleman who held the seat was appointed to an office. If X am correct, that particular case would come under this restriction.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: Unless he resigned before he received the appointment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: It is possible the situation might be brought about that way. I have no objection whatever to accepting the suggestion of the hon. member, and I would move that the Committee rise and report progress. I suppose there would be no objection to carrying the amendment I moved.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: I have no objection.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: A provision might be made to meet the case of a member resigning to accept office.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: I would suggest that we leave the whole question open.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext: It is desirable that the committee should have an opportunity to think over what means we might devise to ameliorate this condition. So far as this measure goes, it is an improvement, because it does in certain cases take the power out of the hands of the Governor in Council of indefinitely retarding elections, and possibly on greater consideration, there may be some reason for a further modification. I should be glad to have the benefit of the views of the hon. gentleman who introduced the Bill, and of consultation with the members of the committee who reported it, before assenting to any change.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.
speechtext:
This is a very good
Bill and is a long step to reform. But we are passing a law fixing the period that must elapse between the occurring of the vacancy and the holding of -the election, and I do not think there is any good reason why the cause of vacancy should have any bearing on the question at all. The important question is: How long should any constituency be left unrepresented? We have decided that six months is long enough, and I do not see the force of the suggestion that we should take into consideration how the vacancy occurs. The important point is that the constituency shall not be left more -than six months without proper steps being taken to give it representation In the House. In one case a man is appointed a judge and' the law permits a period of six months before the constituency may be represented. Another man with capricious notions resigns without any conceivable reason, and it is not fair that his constituency should be penalized and

left unrepresented simply because of his idiosyncr.acy.

subtopic: AMENDMENT AS TO DELAY FOR BYELECTIONS AND DECLARING POLLING DAYS PUBLIC HOLIDAYS.

I recognize the force of my hon. friend's contention, but I have already intimated my willingness to let the matter stand.
